questions.stem: Historians of the period are careful to distinguish the pamphleteer's early polemics, which were merely {1} — forceful, but directed at ministerial policy rather than at persons — from the columns he wrote after 1893, whose {2} abuse of immigrant families was reprinted in provincial papers and poisoned local politics for a generation.
questions.explanation: The dash defines blank 1 as force without malice, which is exactly vehement; benign contradicts "forceful" and noxious would concede the harm the sentence is withholding until later. Blank 2 needs venom that spreads and infects — the reprinting and the "poisoned" politics — so virulent is required; insidious names harm that works secretly, which open printed abuse cannot, and salutary is the opposite of what is described.

questions.stem: The commission attributes the refinery fire less to any single act of negligence than to a culture of improvisation: workers habitually decanted a highly {1} solvent into open trays, trusting that the fumes would disperse, and supervisors treated such {2} of written procedure as proof of initiative rather than as an invitation to disaster.
questions.explanation: Fumes rising from an open tray point to a liquid that evaporates readily and dangerously — the literal chemical sense of volatile; a viscous solvent would sit in the tray, and versatile is only a lookalike. Blank 2 must name the workers' departure from "written procedure," which infractions does, whereas ratifications and vindications would mean the procedure was upheld, leaving nothing for supervisors to excuse.

questions.stem: Reviewers who had lavished praise on his first novel greeted the sequel with attacks so {1} — sneering imputations about the author's marriage and finances rather than any judgment of his prose — that two of the reviewers' own colleagues publicly disavowed them.
questions.explanation: The attacks are personal, poisonous, and shameful enough to be disavowed, so the blank must name venom, not mere energy: virulent and vitriolic are equivalent here. Vehement would describe force alone (one can be vehement in defense of someone) and trenchant would praise the reviews as incisive — both fit the grammar while changing the meaning; perfunctory contradicts the sustained malice and mercurial names inconstancy, not hostility.

questions.stem: With rival militias encamped on either bank of the river and the last food convoy turned back at gunpoint, the border districts remained far too {1} for unarmed monitors to be deployed there.
questions.explanation: The danger is that the situation may erupt into violence at any moment, which is precisely what volatile and combustible convey of a place. Capricious and mercurial describe changeable temperament or whim rather than latent explosion and would be odd of districts; fractious would say only that the districts are quarrelsome, and moribund reverses the sense entirely.

questions.stem: Epidemiologists stress that the 1918 strain was not simply more transmissible than its predecessors but far more {1}: it killed previously healthy adults within days and resisted every treatment then available.
questions.explanation: The sentence sets transmissibility aside and asks for the term of art for a pathogen's destructive power — one that kills fast and defies treatment — which is virulent. Insidious would require a stealthy, gradual onset that "within days" rules out, pernicious likewise suggests slow moral or physical corrosion, endemic speaks to a disease's constant presence in a region rather than its severity, and salubrious is health-giving.
